axes.name: Task Effectiveness & Interaction
axes.description: Evaluates whether users can initiate, progress through, and complete intended tasks efficiently through understandable controls, predictable interaction, timely feedback, resilient forms, recoverable errors, and acceptable runtime responsiveness.
axes.core_question: Can users start, progress through, and complete their intended task efficiently and confidently, with clear controls, timely feedback, and recoverable errors?
look_for: A clear initiation or next action exists where the task requires one.
Interactive controls behave predictably and communicate meaningful state changes.
Forms and input flows avoid unnecessary effort and clearly communicate requirements.
User actions receive timely and understandable system feedback.
Errors can be prevented where practical and recovered from without unnecessary loss of user input or progress.
Users can correct, reverse, retry, or leave actions where appropriate.
Successful task completion or submission is clearly confirmed.
Where runtime evidence exists, loading, responsiveness, and visual stability do not materially interrupt task progress.
healthy_signals: The relevant next action is discoverable when needed.
Controls communicate their purpose, state, and result consistently.
User actions produce timely feedback.
Forms communicate requirements before or at the point of input.
Recoverable errors preserve useful user-entered data where possible.
Error feedback explains how to recover.
Users can correct or reverse actions where appropriate.
Completion states clearly explain what happened and what happens next.
Available runtime evidence shows no major performance friction that materially disrupts the task.
failure_modes: The relevant primary or next action is difficult to identify.
Controls behave unpredictably or provide unclear state feedback.
The user cannot determine whether an action succeeded.
Forms impose avoidable effort or lose entered information.
Error states describe failure without enabling recovery.
Users become trapped or cannot correct an important mistake.
Task completion is ambiguous.
Loading, interaction delay, or layout instability materially interrupts progress.
out_of_scope: Site-wide information taxonomy or destination organization.
Pure wording quality unless wording directly causes interaction ambiguity.
Whether the product solves the correct strategic problem.
User satisfaction or emotional response inferred without user evidence.

severity_ladder.high: The issue prevents or seriously threatens completion of an important task, causes unrecoverable loss, blocks an essential control, or creates substantial repeated failure with no reasonable workaround.
severity_ladder.medium: The issue materially increases task effort, uncertainty, error likelihood, or recovery cost, but a reasonable workaround remains.
severity_ladder.low: The issue creates localized friction or unnecessary effort without substantially threatening successful completion.

evidence_expectations: Identify the affected task, control, form, or state.
Show the observable interaction or runtime condition.
Distinguish actual runtime evidence from visual inference.
Include before/after state where interaction behavior is relevant.
Performance claims identify whether evidence is laboratory, browser-runtime, or field data.
Do not call Lighthouse lab measurements field Core Web Vitals.
axes.default_fix: Make the relevant action and state clear, simplify avoidable task friction, provide timely feedback, preserve recoverable progress, and make completion or recovery explicit.
axes.business_impact: Task friction can increase abandonment, support demand, user errors, failed transactions or processes, and operational cost.
axes.user_impact: Users may spend more effort, make more mistakes, lose progress, or fail to complete the intended task.

axes.name: Information Architecture & Navigation
axes.description: Evaluates whether information, destinations, and functional areas are organized and exposed in a way that supports findability, orientation, and confident navigation through the product.
axes.core_question: Can users understand how information and destinations are organized, know where they are, and confidently choose where to go next?
look_for: Navigation categories and destinations are organized coherently.
Navigation labels provide enough information scent to predict their destinations.
Related information and functionality are grouped meaningfully.
Important destinations are discoverable from expected locations.
Users can determine their current location, scope, or context where orientation is needed.
Comparable pages or screens use consistent navigation mechanisms.
Parent-child and section relationships are understandable.
Excessive hierarchy depth, fragmentation, duplication, or disconnected destinations do not create avoidable search effort.
Destination content confirms what the selected navigation path suggested.
healthy_signals: Repeated navigation appears in a predictable order and uses familiar labels.
Sectioning, grouping, and layout help users scan from overview to detail.
The page sequence supports evaluation, trust-building, and conversion without dead ends.
failure_modes: Navigation is visually present but does not explain where important information lives.
Section order follows the company's internal logic instead of the buyer's decision flow.
Different areas of the journey feel disconnected, making users re-orient on every page.
The interface hides key destinations behind generic labels, weak hierarchy, or fragmented page structure.
out_of_scope: Do not criticize missing pages or hidden global navigation that is not visible in the provided evidence.
Do not infer broken IA from one unconventional layout if orientation still remains clear.

severity_ladder.high: Users would struggle to understand where to go, what page they are on, or how the offer is organized.
severity_ladder.medium: The structure is usable, but visible wayfinding and grouping choices create avoidable orientation cost.
severity_ladder.low: The journey is understandable, with only minor scan or grouping inefficiencies.

evidence_expectations: Reference visible navigation labels, section titles, breadcrumb-like cues, or grouping patterns.
Explain how the visible order either supports or interrupts the buyer's likely path.
axes.default_fix: Clarify destination structure and navigation labels, group related information coherently, expose important destinations in expected locations, and strengthen orientation cues.
axes.business_impact: Poor architecture and navigation can reduce discoverability of important functionality or information, increase abandonment and support demand, and make products harder to learn.
axes.user_impact: Users may search repeatedly, choose incorrect destinations, lose orientation, or fail to find needed information or functionality.

axes.name: Accessibility
axes.description: Evaluates observable barriers that may prevent people with disabilities from perceiving, understanding, navigating, or operating the interface, using WCAG 2.2 and applicable platform accessibility guidance as the primary reference.
axes.core_question: Can people with diverse abilities perceive, understand, navigate, and operate the audited interface without avoidable accessibility barriers?
look_for: WCAG 2.2 contrast and non-text contrast risks detected from rendered foreground/background measurements.
WCAG 2.2 keyboard, focus order, and focus-visible risks detected from runtime tab traversal when available.
WCAG 2.2 name/role/value, link-purpose, target-size, label, and instruction risks detected from controls and forms.
Applicable target-size requirements, semantic structure, meaningful relationships, accessible status feedback, and observable motion or input-modality barriers.
healthy_signals: Text and controls meet WCAG contrast thresholds on the captured pages.
Tab order reaches visible controls in a logical order and focus is visibly identifiable.
Links, buttons, and form fields have clear accessible names and work when activated.
failure_modes: Low-contrast text or controls fail WCAG 2.2 readability/non-text contrast expectations.
Controls are unreachable by keyboard, have weak focus indicators, or fail when activated.
Links, buttons, and fields have missing/ambiguous accessible names, labels, or instructions.
Targets are too small, motion is distracting, or a drawer/modal creates a keyboard or operation barrier.
out_of_scope: Do not claim screen-reader output beyond accessible-name, role, label, and DOM evidence captured by the audit.
Do not invent keyboard failures when the keyboard probe was not run; mark missing runtime coverage as a limitation.

severity_ladder.high: A verified barrier prevents or seriously obstructs access to essential content, navigation, or functionality, especially where no reasonable alternative is available.
severity_ladder.medium: A verified barrier creates material difficulty for a meaningful group of users but does not completely prevent the affected task or content.
severity_ladder.low: A localized accessibility problem has limited scope or impact while still violating an applicable requirement or accessibility expectation.

evidence_expectations: Cite the WCAG 2.2 success criterion number, measured signal, affected page, and exact visible control or text sample.
Prefer runtime evidence from Playwright, contrast calculations, accessible names, target sizes, and keyboard tab probes.
axes.default_fix: Correct the cited accessibility barrier using the applicable standard or platform guidance, then retest the affected element or task using relevant automated, keyboard, visual, or assistive-technology evidence.
axes.business_impact: Accessibility barriers can exclude users, create compliance and legal risk, increase support burden, and prevent access to important services or functionality.
axes.user_impact: People with disabilities may be unable to perceive content, understand controls, navigate the interface, or complete essential tasks.

axes.name: Visual Hierarchy & Interface Consistency
axes.description: Evaluates whether visual emphasis, layout, typography, spacing, and recurring interface components form a coherent system that makes priority, relationships, and expected patterns easy to recognize.
axes.core_question: Does the interface guide attention to what matters and apply coherent, predictable visual and component patterns across comparable surfaces?
look_for: Visual emphasis reflects intended information and action priority.
Heading and content levels are visually distinguishable.
Related items are perceptually grouped.
Equivalent components use coherent appearance and state treatment.
Typography follows a recognizable hierarchy.
Spacing and alignment use repeatable patterns.
Color and visual states are applied consistently.
Comparable pages or screens use coherent layouts and component families.
Responsive variants preserve important hierarchy and relationships.
healthy_signals: Component families feel related through spacing, shape, hierarchy, and behavior cues.
Repeated navigation, CTA, and form patterns stay visually and semantically aligned.
The experience looks intentionally systemized rather than assembled screen by screen.
failure_modes: Equivalent actions look unrelated or switch labels, tone, or emphasis across contexts.
Spacing, typography, or card treatments vary enough to weaken predictability and polish.
One section or page looks like a different product, forcing the user to re-evaluate what is interactive.
The UI mixes conventions in a way that makes repeated use less efficient.
out_of_scope: Do not force visual sameness when a difference clearly communicates state or priority.
Do not over-penalize brand-led variation unless it breaks predictability or recognition.

severity_ladder.high: Visible inconsistency makes the product feel immature, unreliable, or cognitively expensive to use.
severity_ladder.medium: Most patterns work, but recurring inconsistency would slow trust-building and repeated use.
severity_ladder.low: The interface is coherent overall, with only localized or cosmetic inconsistency.

evidence_expectations: Compare at least two visible examples when claiming inconsistency.
Name the component family or repeated pattern that changes across contexts.
axes.default_fix: Normalize hierarchy, repeated components, typography, spacing, alignment, and state treatments so equivalent information and actions are visually predictable.
axes.business_impact: Inconsistent interface patterns can increase learning cost, design and maintenance overhead, user errors, and perceived product immaturity.
axes.user_impact: Users may struggle to identify priority, interpret relationships, or transfer learned interaction patterns between similar screens.

axes.name: Content Clarity & Guidance
axes.description: Evaluates whether visible language helps users understand information, choices, actions, requirements, consequences, and recovery without unnecessary interpretation or jargon.
axes.core_question: Can users understand what the interface is telling them, what available actions mean, and what they need to do next?
look_for: Headings describe the content that follows.
Buttons and action labels communicate the intended action.
Link text provides meaningful destination or action context.
Labels use understandable and consistent terminology.
Instructions and helper text clarify meaningful requirements.
Error messages explain what happened and how to recover.
Important terminology, status, confirmation, and consequences are clear and consistent.
Important information can be scanned efficiently.
healthy_signals: Headings answer user questions quickly and match the visible action path.
CTA and control labels use familiar, concrete language tied to an outcome.
Required instructions, helper text, and reassurance appear where the user needs them.
failure_modes: Headlines are generic, clever, or internally focused rather than buyer-facing.
Buttons, labels, or helper text force users to guess what a control means or what comes next.
Copy is dense, repetitive, or vague enough to weaken scanning and comprehension.
Jargon appears without explanation, or the page talks about the company without clarifying user value.
out_of_scope: Do not infer a weak proposition from missing business context if the visible copy is still clear and specific.
Do not flag every short heading as weak when the surrounding copy and CTA provide enough meaning.

severity_ladder.high: The visible wording makes the product, action, or value proposition hard to understand.
severity_ladder.medium: The copy is understandable, but vague, generic, or inconsistent enough to slow decision-making.
severity_ladder.low: The wording is mostly clear, with only localized wording or tone improvements needed.

evidence_expectations: Quote the actual heading, label, or CTA text that supports the finding.
Explain what a first-time visitor would still not understand after reading the visible copy.
axes.default_fix: Rewrite the affected wording using concise, consistent user-facing language that clearly communicates meaning, action, requirements, consequences, and recovery.
axes.business_impact: Unclear language can increase errors, abandonment, support demand, misinterpretation, and failed task completion.
axes.user_impact: Users may misunderstand available choices, requirements, consequences, or recovery steps and spend unnecessary effort interpreting the interface.
